newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Sugar spike seen if Australia cyclone strikes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Sugar spike seen if Australia cyclone strikes.

text.p: World sugar prices were likely to spike if cyclone Justin hit the sugar-cane crop in the Australian state of Queensland, brokers and sugar industrey executives said on Tuesday.
One commodities broker said significant damage to the Australian sugar crop was likely to cause world prices to "skyrocket".

On Tuesday afternoon Australian weather forecasters said cyclone Justin remained stationary about 620 km off Cairns and was beginning to decline in power as the sea cooled. Cyclone warnings along the Queensland coast were lifted.

Australia, two years ago the world's biggest exporter of sugar, now rates number three, marginally after Thailand and Brazil. All three countries produce about five million tonnes of raw sugar a year.

Michael Bosscher, deputy chief executive of Queensland Sugar Corp, which produces all of Queensland's annual sugar crop, said that even if the entire current sugarcane crop were wiped out, he could not see world prices rising to 20 cents a lb. The world sugar price presently languishes at 11 US cents a lb compared with 45 US cents a lb in 1979,
"(But) conceptually the broker is right," Bosscher said.
"If there's significant damage done to the Queensland crop, it might provide a bit of a spike. Nothing major and not sustainable, a nervous reaction," he said.
Australia's five million tonnes of raw sugar annual production compared with world production of 125 million tonnes, he pointed out.
To wipe out Queensland's entire sugarcane crop, a cyclone would have to travel 2,500 km of coastline, from north of Cairns to the New South Wales border, "wiping out every bit", he said.
QSC always assured its customers that all of the Queensland coast would never be affected by adverse weather at the same time, he said.
